extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and educated readers interested in political theory and comparative public finance (19th-century focus)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for assessing how democratic governments manage public expenditure, salaries, corruption, and capacity for sustained effort, with comparative remarks (principally USA vs France).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendencies of democracies regarding salaries of public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies those who establish high salaries have no chance of profiting by them. The people fixes the salaries of the public officers, and the scale of remuneration is determined by the consideration of its own wants; it is held fair that servants of the public should be placed in the same easy circumstances as the public itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed effects: democratic states are parsimonious toward principal agents (higher functionaries) but pay secondary officers relatively well. The poor cannot conceive the wants of higher classes, so sums scanty to the rich appear enormous to the poor; secondary officers being nearly on a level with the people excite interest, while higher officers arouse envy. Example data: comparative salary table for US vs France (messenger, clerks, chief clerk, secretary, president/king).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of public expenditure between community services and remuneration to rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy gives largely to the community, and very sparingly to those who govern it; in aristocracies the money of the state is expended to the profit of the persons who are at the head of affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: a democratic state's apparent economy toward principal officers has led to an exaggerated view of its thrift; although it may not allow means of honorable subsistence to conductors, enormous sums may be lavished to meet exigencies or to facilitate the enjoyments of the people (e.g., maintenance of the poor, gratuitous instruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish institutional causes of economy from manners and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether a people's government is economical, carefully distinguish that economy which depends upon institutions from that which is the natural result of their manners and customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Americans' dislike of public rejoicings, indifference to ornament in architecture, or commercial habits may produce frugality in public expenditure independent of democratic institutions. Investigators should separate legal/political causes from social habits when attributing causes of economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminaries required to estimate public charges: national wealth and rate of taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate the extent of public charges two preliminaries are indispensable: (1) to know the wealth of the people; and (2) to learn what portion of that wealth is devoted to the expenditure of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth consists of population, real property, and personal property; population is usually obtainable but property values are difficult to determine. Showing taxation without showing the resources (wealth) is futile because the relation of expenditure to revenue is the meaningful metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for differences in scope and levels of government when comparing expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Budgets at different government levels (central/union, departments/states, counties, townships, municipal divisions) embrace different objects; direct comparisons between countries (e.g., France and the United States) require aligning comparable scopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Union's budget covers fewer objects than France's central government; American townships discharge offices reserved to departments or the state in France. One must decide which level (national, departmental/state, municipal) to compare and account for functions that may be assigned differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-monetary contributions and obligations in measuring public burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments not only demand supplies of money but also call for personal services which are equivalent to a given sum (e.g., militia or army service); accurate comparison must account for these contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a soldier's time has value and should be treated as a tax; many other instances of in-kind or service contributions exist and their relative amounts across countries are difficult to estimate but materially affect comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external qualitative signs of prosperity as proxies when statistics are lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of accurate accounts one may judge the proportion taxation bears to prosperity by observing external signs: whether the country appears flourishing, whether poor retain subsistence and rich means of enjoyment after taxes, and whether both classes are contented yet striving to improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an observer sees retained means, contentment, ongoing industry and capital employment, they can infer taxation is relatively light. The author applies this to conclude Americans contribute a smaller portion of income to the state than French citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware misleading precision when statistics are inaccurate
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics not founded upon strictly accurate computations mislead instead of guiding; the false affectation of exactitude can disguise error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion: abandon numerical investigations when data are insufficient and prefer cautious qualitative assessment or seek other kinds of data rather than forcing flawed numeric comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative perseverance and continuity as determinants of government economy
rubrics_metrics.description: A government's lack of perseverance in undertakings and absence of steady control over employed agents causes ill-conducted or unfinished projects, leading to disproportionate spending or unprofitable expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic tendencies to frequently change designs and remove agents produce ill-conducted projects and wasted expenditure; stability and continuity in administration reduce waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's propensity to increase expenditures for popular benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the poor direct public affairs and dispose of national resources, they are apt to augment public expenditure to meet their own benefits (maintenance of the poor, public instruction, remuneration of services, liberal pay to subordinate agents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: democratic governments may be expensive not because they are wasteful in elite remuneration but because they expand services and benefits to the populace; this should be taken into account when judging overall economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and societal effects of corruption differ by regime
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracies rulers sometimes endeavor to corrupt the people; in democracies rulers frequently show themselves to be corrupt. In the former their vices are directly prejudicial to the morality of the people; in the latter their indirect influence is often more pernicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocratic corruption may be refined and hidden, limiting spread; democratic corruption—visible pillage of the public purse and sale of favors—is more comprehensible and contagious, lending government authority to base practices and fostering vicious ambition among citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socioeconomic status of rulers affects susceptibility to corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocratic governments rulers are often rich and thus less craving for money; in democracies statesmen are often poor and have fortunes to make, making them more open to suspicion of dishonorable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the poverty-driven ambition of democratic leaders may produce public examples that encourage corruption among citizens who see peers rise quickly to power and wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic capacity for sustained national effort (war/conscription)
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic people is less capable of sustained effort than others: practices like conscription or impressment of seamen are difficult or unknown in America, and prolonged war sacrifices and heavy taxation are harder to impose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: the US during the war of independence showed initial zeal but later private egotism, poor recruitment, empty treasuries, and reluctance to endure privations; to test democratic capacity one would need to see willingness to commit large fractions of income or population as in European states.
